destination.title: He Had No Lawyer. So He Wrote the Supreme Court in Pencil.

short02: If you can't afford a lawyer, does the court just give you one for free?
One man was charged with a crime.
Too poor to hire a lawyer, he asked for one and was told no.
From his cell, with a pencil, he wrote a petition to the Supreme Court.
In 1963, nine to zero: if you can't pay, the state must give you a lawyer.
One handwritten letter changed courtrooms across America.
Watch the full story on the channel.

candidate_payload_lines: In 1963, almost no one in America had heard the name Clarence Earl Gideon.
The Sixth Amendment promises anyone accused of a crime "the assistance of counsel" — the help of a lawyer .
If you have ever heard the phrase "a public defender will be assigned to you," that system traces back, in large part, to a prisoner's pencil .
When a suspect is told, "if you cannot afford a lawyer, one will be appointed for you," those words are not a courtesy.
"You have the right to an attorney" is not set dressing.
And it exists because of one stubborn prisoner, one handwritten letter, and one unanimous decision in 1963 .
Over the next twelve minutes: how a man nobody believed in forced the Supreme Court to rewrite the rules of every criminal trial in America — and the imperfect system that ruling left behind.
But Gideon has one move left that no one expects — and it costs five cents.
On March 18, 1963, the Supreme Court answered — and this time the answer was not close.
A real defense attorney picked the case apart — testing the witnesses, poking at the state's story, doing all the things Gideon had never known how to do alone.
Clarence Earl Gideon got the ending you almost never get.
But the thing he really won was never just for him.
It is a promise paid for by a prisoner with a pencil — powerful, real, and still, to this day, unfinished.

shorts.type: B - the wall he had to ask the Court to knock down
shorts.avoids: short02 tells the pencil-letter story and the 9-0 result. It never mentions that binding precedent said the opposite, or that the Court then handed him one of the finest lawyers in America.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: Thousands of prisoners write to the Supreme Court every year. Why did the justices take this one letter?

lines.text: Twenty years before that letter, the Supreme Court had already looked at almost exactly his question. And it had ruled the other way.
source_lines: Twenty years earlier, in a case called Betts v. Brady, the Supreme Court had already looked at almost this exact question — and had ruled the other way

lines.text: Under that rule a free lawyer came only in special circumstances. If you were very young, or could not read, or the case was unusually complex.
source_lines: A free lawyer was required only in "special circumstances" — if you were very young, or could not read, or the case was unusually complex

lines.text: An ordinary poor man, in an ordinary case, was expected to manage on his own.
source_lines: An ordinary poor man, in an ordinary case, was expected to manage on his own.

lines.text: So he was asking the most powerful court in the country to admit it had been wrong. Prisoners send it thousands of these petitions a year. Almost all are turned away.
source_lines: He is asking the most powerful court in the country to admit it had been wrong — to overturn its own decision and rewrite the rule for every state at once.
Prisoners send the Supreme Court thousands of these handwritten petitions every year.
The Court turns away almost all of them.

lines.text: Gideon had asked the Florida judge for a lawyer and been told no. Free counsel came only in death penalty cases.
source_lines: So he asks the court to appoint a lawyer for him.
in Florida at that time, a free lawyer was provided only when a person's life was on the line, in a death-penalty case

lines.text: He faced a prosecutor who knew every rule by heart, argued his own case, and was convicted. Five years.
source_lines: On one side stands a prosecutor who has done this hundreds of times, who knows every one of those rules by heart.
The verdict comes back guilty, and the court sends him to prison for five years.

lines.text: From his cell he filed as a pauper, too poor to pay, with no firm and no famous attorney behind him.
source_lines: He cannot pay the court's fees, so he files as what the law calls a pauper
No firm is behind him. No famous attorney is making calls.

lines.text: It did not turn away his. One handwritten letter from a Florida prison cell, and the justices agreed to hear the case.

shorts.angle: Winning at the Supreme Court did not set him free. It sent him back to the same courtroom to be tried all over again.
shorts.type: A - same man, same charge, opposite verdict
shorts.avoids: short02 stops at the 1963 ruling and the public defender system. It never says Gideon was retried, or that with a lawyer in the chair the same jury question came back the other way.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: The Court could create the right with a stroke of a pen. Who was ever going to pay for it?

lines.text: Winning at the Supreme Court did not set Clarence Gideon free. It threw out his conviction and sent him back to Florida for a brand new trial.
source_lines: Because winning at the Supreme Court did not set Gideon free.
it threw out his conviction and sent him back to Florida for a brand-new trial

lines.text: The same charges. The same town. But this time, the empty chair was filled.
source_lines: The same charges. The same town. But this time, the empty chair was filled.

lines.text: A real defense attorney picked the case apart. Testing the witnesses, poking at the state's story, doing all the things Gideon had never known how to do alone.
source_lines: A real defense attorney picked the case apart — testing the witnesses, poking at the state's story, doing all the things Gideon had never known how to do alone.

lines.text: The very same man. The very same accusation. Alone, he was convicted and sent to prison. With a lawyer, he was acquitted and walked out free.
source_lines: The very same man, facing the very same accusation.
Alone, he was convicted and sent to prison.
With a lawyer, he was acquitted and walked out free

lines.text: The ruling behind that second trial was unanimous. Every justice agreed that a lawyer is a necessity, not a frill.
source_lines: The decision was unanimous.
a lawyer is not a frill.
A lawyer is a necessity

lines.text: It reached back and overruled its own precedent, leaving one plain rule. Too poor to hire a lawyer, the state appoints one.
source_lines: It reached back and overruled its own precedent.
The new rule was simple enough for anyone to understand: if you are too poor to hire a lawyer, the state must appoint one for you

lines.text: Through the Fourteenth Amendment it bound the states too, so the right could not stop at the federal courthouse door.
source_lines: Through the Fourteenth Amendment, it binds the states too
And because a fair trial is a basic right, the Court held, that right cannot stop at the federal courthouse door.

lines.text: Nothing about him had changed. The only thing that changed was whether anyone in that room was standing on his side.
source_lines: The only thing that changed was whether anyone in that room was standing on his side.
